name: Tashiding
tagline: A hilltop monastery between two rivers, home of the Bumchu vase
meta_description: Tashiding, West Sikkim: the 1641 hilltop monastery, the Bumchu sacred-water festival, mani stones, chortens, how to reach from Yuksom or Pelling, 2026 costs.
summary: Tashiding is a small town below a hilltop monastery at 1,465 m, between the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet. The monastery was founded in 1641 by Ngadak Sempa Chenpo, one of the three lamas who crowned Sikkim's first king. It is about 19 km from Yuksom and 40 km from Pelling, ideal for a half-day trip.
intro: Tashiding is a quiet bazaar town on the road between Legship and Yuksom, and above it, on a hilltop between two rivers, stands one of Sikkim's most sacred monasteries. The Rathong Chu comes down from the Kangchenjunga side and meets the Rangeet below the hill. The monastery sits at about 1,465 m, surrounded by chortens, prayer flags and old trees. The name is usually explained as 'the devoted central glory', and the site is also called Drakkar Tashiding.

Most travellers come for a few hours. You can visit from Yuksom, about 19 km and an hour away, or from Pelling, about 40 km and 1.5–2 hours via Legship. The monastery itself has a main temple, a large field of chortens and long rows of stone slabs carved with the mantra 'Om Mani Padme Hum'. There is no big ticket queue and no shopping arcade. It is a working religious site, and it feels like one.

Once a year Tashiding fills up. On the 14th and 15th days of the first Tibetan month, usually in February or March, the Bumchu festival draws pilgrims from across Sikkim and beyond to see the sacred vase opened and its water read as an omen for the year. If you visit then, book early and expect crowds. At other times, you may have the hilltop almost to yourself, with only monks, pilgrims and the wind in the flags.

story.title: The vase that tells Sikkim its future
paras: Tashiding was founded in 1641 by Ngadak Sempa Chenpo, one of the three Nyingma lamas who met at Yuksom and crowned Phuntsog Namgyal the first Chogyal in 1642. It was extended and renovated in 1717 during the reign of the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal. Tradition tells that three monks saw a bright light shining on the top of Kangchenjunga, reflected onto this hill, and heard divine music. They built a small chorten there, the Thongwa Rang Drol, which it is said frees anyone who simply sees it.

The monastery is best known for a sacred vase. Tradition holds that Guru Padmasambhava blessed a vase of water gathered from holy places in India and beyond, and that it was later found and placed at Tashiding. Each year, on the 14th and 15th days of the first Tibetan month, lamas open the vase in front of the crowd. According to Wikipedia's account of the Bhumchu festival, if the water is full there will be peace and plenty; if it overflows, disturbance; if it is low, famine.

After the reading, the lamas share a little of the water with devotees, then top up the vase with river water and seal it again for the next year. In 2026 the festival fell on 3 March. For pilgrims it is the most important day of the year here, and people walk up the hill in long lines carrying bottles for the blessed water. Visitors are welcome, but this is a religious rite, not a show, so be respectful.
story.source: Wikipedia: 'Tashiding Monastery', 'Bhumchu', 'History of Sikkim'; the founding light and the vase's origin are traditional accounts

did_you_know: The flagstones around Tashiding Monastery were carved with 'Om Mani Padme Hum' by a craftsman named Yanchong Lodil.
Wikipedia lists 41 chortens of different kinds at Tashiding Monastery.

highlights.title: Tashiding Monastery
highlights.text: Founded in 1641 by Ngadak Sempa Chenpo and enlarged in 1717, Tashiding is one of Sikkim's most sacred Nyingma monasteries. It sits on a hilltop at 1,465 m between the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet. Come in the morning, when prayers are on and the hill is quiet.

highlights.title: The Bumchu festival
highlights.text: On the 14th and 15th days of the first Tibetan month, usually February or March, lamas open the sacred vase and read its water level as an omen for Sikkim's year. Thousands of pilgrims come for the blessed water. In 2026 it fell on 3 March; check current status for future dates.

highlights.title: Mani stones and chortens
highlights.text: Rows of stone slabs carved with 'Om Mani Padme Hum', and a field of chortens of many shapes and sizes, surround the main temple. Walk among them clockwise, slowly, and look for the carving detail. Wikipedia counts 41 chortens at the monastery.

highlights.title: Thongwa Rang Drol chorten
highlights.text: Tradition says that simply seeing this chorten frees a person, which is how it got its name. It was, the story goes, the first structure on the hill, built by monks who saw light from Kangchenjunga shining here. Ask a monk or caretaker to point it out.

highlights.title: A link in the pilgrim circuit
highlights.text: Tashiding is part of West Sikkim's old Buddhist circuit with Yuksom, Dubdi, Pemayangtse and Khecheopalri Lake. It is about 19 km from Yuksom and 40 km from Pelling, so it fits into a Pelling–Yuksom trip with half a day to spare.

highlights.title: Kirateshwar temple at Legship
highlights.text: On the Pelling road at Legship, the Kirateshwar Mahadev Temple stands on the bank of the Rangeet. Hindu tradition says Shiva appeared to Arjuna here as the hunter Kirateshwar. It is a short stop that shows how Hindu and Buddhist sacred sites sit side by side in West Sikkim.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps run from Gyalshing to Tashiding for about ₹100–150 a seat, indicative, 2026. Reach Gyalshing first by shared jeep from Pelling (₹50–80), Siliguri (₹400–550) or Gangtok (₹350–500). Departures to Tashiding are limited, so ask at the Gyalshing stand the evening before. Check current status before you travel.

Tashiding is about 40 km from Pelling via Legship, 1.5–2 hours, and about 19 km from Yuksom, around an hour. A reserved car is the easiest way to combine Tashiding with Yuksom or Pelling in a day. Agree the route, waiting time and fare before you set off; fares are higher than the standard Pelling loops.

The nearest railhead is New Jalpaiguri (NJP) and the nearest reliable airport is Bagdogra (IXB). From either, the road runs via Melli, Jorethang and Legship, about 5.5–6.5 hours. Most visitors stay in Pelling or Yuksom and visit Tashiding on a day trip. Check road status in the monsoon.

where_to_stay: Tashiding has a few simple lodges and homestays around the bazaar, useful if you want to be on the hill for the Bumchu festival or start early. They are basic: clean rooms, shared or simple attached bathrooms, and home-style food. Most travellers base themselves elsewhere. In Yuksom, an hour away, Hotel Yangrigang and family homestays are good budget choices. In Pelling, 1.5–2 hours away, the options run from Hotel Garuda and Norbu Ghang Resort to the Elgin Mount Pandim and the Chumbi Mountain Retreat. For Bumchu, book anything near Tashiding weeks ahead.
budget_tip: Visit Tashiding on the way between Yuksom and Pelling rather than as a separate trip from Pelling; adding it to a route you are already driving costs far less than a dedicated return car.
tips: Walk clockwise around the monastery, chortens and mani stones, and do not sit or step on the carved slabs.
Dress modestly, remove your shoes at shrine doors and ask before taking photographs inside.
For Bumchu, arrive the day before, carry a small bottle for the blessed water and expect long queues; check current status for dates.
Carry water and snacks; the hilltop has few shops, and the bazaar below has the only real choice of food.
In the monsoon the Legship–Tashiding road can be blocked by landslides, so keep a spare day; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Bumchu sacred-water festival
experiences.cost: Free; budget for stay and transport, indicative
experiences.summary: Once a year, lamas at Tashiding open a sacred vase and read its water level as an omen for Sikkim's coming year. Pilgrims arrive from across Sikkim and beyond to receive a few drops of the blessed water. It is the biggest day of the year here, and visitors are welcome to watch respectfully.
body: The name Bumchu joins bum, a vase, and chu, water, and the festival is held on the 14th and 15th days of the first month of the Tibetan calendar, which usually falls in February or March. In 2026 it fell on 3 March. Tradition holds that Guru Padmasambhava blessed the vase, filled with water from holy places, and that it was later brought to Tashiding. The ceremony has been held here for generations, and it is one of the most important events in Sikkim's Buddhist year.

During the ceremony the lamas open the sealed vase and check the water. According to Wikipedia, if it is full, the year will bring peace and plenty; if it overflows, disturbance; and if it is low, famine. A little water is then shared with the waiting crowd, the vase is topped up with river water and sealed again for the next year. There are prayers and music through the day, and long lines of pilgrims climb the hill.

If you plan to go, arrive the day before and stay in Tashiding, Yuksom or Pelling. Rooms near Tashiding are few and fill fast, so book weeks ahead. Dress warmly, as nights are cold, and carry water, snacks and a small bottle if you hope to receive the blessed water. Keep to the edges of the crowd, do not push and do not use a flash. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the Bumchu festival in Tashiding
faqs.a: Bumchu is held on the 14th and 15th days of the first month of the Tibetan calendar, usually in February or March. In 2026 the main day fell on 3 March. Because the date follows the lunar calendar, it changes each year. Check current status with Sikkim Tourism or a local contact before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens at the Bumchu festival
faqs.a: Lamas open a sacred vase kept at Tashiding Monastery and read the water level as an omen: full means peace and plenty, overflowing means disturbance, and low means famine. They share a little of the water with devotees, then top up the vase with river water and seal it again for the next year.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend Bumchu at Tashiding
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors are welcome to watch the Bumchu festival as long as they are respectful. Dress modestly, stay at the edges of the crowd, do not push towards the vase and avoid flash photography. Rooms near Tashiding are limited, so book well ahead or stay in Yuksom or Pelling and arrive early.

experiences.title: Mani stone and chorten circuit
experiences.summary: A slow, clockwise walk around Tashiding Monastery's main temple, its field of chortens and its long rows of stone slabs carved with 'Om Mani Padme Hum'. Look for the Thongwa Rang Drol chorten, which tradition says frees anyone who sees it, and the views down to the two rivers.
body: Start at the main temple. Tashiding was founded in 1641 by Ngadak Sempa Chenpo, one of the three lamas of the Yuksom coronation, and extended in 1717 under the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal. If the doors are open, step inside quietly, remove your shoes and ask before taking photographs. Morning prayers are the best time to visit. Afterwards, follow the path that leads out to the chortens and carved stones around the hilltop.

The field of chortens is the heart of the site. Wikipedia counts 41 chortens of different kinds here, some old and weathered, some freshly whitewashed. Tradition says the Thongwa Rang Drol chorten, among the first structures on the hill, frees anyone who simply sees it. Around the monastery lie flagstones carved with 'Om Mani Padme Hum', the work of a craftsman named Yanchong Lodil. Walk past them clockwise, keeping them on your right, and never step on them.

Take your time. This is a place for slow walking, not ticking boxes. From the edge of the hilltop you look down to the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet, and on clear days to the forested ridges towards Yuksom and Pelling. There is no fixed fee that we know of; a small donation at the temple is welcome. Bring water and a snack, and leave nothing behind but your footprints.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Tashiding Monastery
faqs.a: We are not aware of a fixed entry fee for Tashiding Monastery. Visitors usually leave a small donation at the temple. Parking or local charges may apply near the hill, and rules can change, especially during the Bumchu festival. Check current status before you travel, and carry small notes for donations and snacks.

faqs.q: What are mani stones
faqs.a: Mani stones are flat stones or slabs carved with Buddhist mantras, most often 'Om Mani Padme Hum', the mantra of Avalokiteśvara. At Tashiding, the flagstones around the monastery were carved by a craftsman named Yanchong Lodil. Pilgrims walk past them clockwise as an act of devotion, and visitors should never step or sit on them.

faqs.q: How long does it take to see Tashiding Monastery
faqs.a: Allow 1.5–2 hours for the main temple, the chortens and the mani stones at a gentle pace, plus time to reach the top from where vehicles stop. With travel, a visit from Yuksom takes about half a day, and from Pelling most of a day, especially if you add Legship on the way.

experiences.title: Ridge walk above the Rathong Chu and Rangeet
experiences.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, Oct–May
experiences.summary: Tashiding's hill rises between two rivers, the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet. A slow walk along the hilltop and the village lanes below gives long views down to the valleys, terraced fields and forest. It is free, quiet and a good way to understand why monks chose this spot.
body: The monastery stands on top of a hill rising between the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet. The Rathong Chu comes down from the high Kangchenjunga side, past the forests of the national park, and the Rangeet runs on south to Legship and Jorethang before joining the Teesta at Melli. From the edges of the hilltop you see the valleys open on either side, with terraced fields, cardamom groves and forest falling steeply to the water.

Start after your monastery visit and walk the paths around the hilltop, then wander down through the village lanes towards the bazaar. You do not need a fixed route. Stop wherever the view opens up, and look out for prayer flags strung across the slopes. Early morning brings mist lifting from the river valleys; late afternoon brings warm light on the ridges. On clear days in autumn and winter the hills towards Yuksom and Pelling stand out sharply.

Wear comfortable shoes, as paths are steep and uneven, and ask locally before following any trail that leads well down towards the rivers, since some are steep and not maintained. Carry water and keep to paths that villagers use. Respect fields and private land, and greet people as you pass. The walk costs nothing and gives you a feel for Tashiding as a living village, not only a monastery. End it with tea in the bazaar.

faqs.q: Which rivers flow below Tashiding
faqs.a: Tashiding Monastery stands on a hilltop between the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet. The Rathong Chu comes down from the Kangchenjunga side, and the Rangeet flows south past Legship and Jorethang to join the Teesta at Melli. From the hilltop you can see both valleys on clear days.

faqs.q: Can I walk down to the river from Tashiding
faqs.a: There are village paths down the slopes, but some are steep, rough and not maintained, and the river banks can be dangerous, especially in the monsoon when water rises fast. Ask locally before following any path towards the rivers, and never go alone. For most visitors, the views from the hilltop and village lanes are enough.

faqs.q: Is Tashiding good for photography
faqs.a: Yes. The chortens, prayer flags and carved mani stones make strong subjects, and the hilltop looks over two river valleys. Early morning mist and late afternoon light are best. Ask before photographing people or inside the temple, avoid flash, and be especially careful during the Bumchu festival, when crowds are large.

experiences.title: Kirateshwar Mahadev Temple stop at Legship
experiences.summary: On the road between Pelling and Tashiding, the Kirateshwar Mahadev Temple at Legship stands on the bank of the Rangeet. Hindu tradition says Shiva appeared to Arjuna here as the hunter Kirateshwar. It is a short, easy stop that pairs a Hindu riverside temple with Tashiding's Buddhist hilltop on the same day.
body: Legship is a small junction town on the Rangeet, where roads to Pelling, Gyalshing, Tashiding, Yuksom and Gangtok meet. Its name comes from the Lepcha word for a kind of fern, from the jungle that once covered the area. On the river bank stands the Kirateshwar Mahadev Temple, described as one of the holiest and oldest Shiva temples in Sikkim. The Kirati people call it Kirateshwar Mahadev Thaan, and locals often just say Shiv Mandir.

Hindu tradition says Arjuna did penance here, and Shiva appeared to him as a hunter, Kirateshwar, and blessed him with success in the Mahabharata war. The main object of worship is a stone revered as a Shiva linga, and the complex also has shrines to Rama and Durga. Devotees believe a sincere visit fulfils wishes. Two festivals bring crowds: Bala Chaturdashi in November or December, and Maha Shivaratri in February or March.

For travellers, it is an easy stop of under an hour on the drive between Pelling and Tashiding. Remove your shoes, dress modestly and follow the lead of local devotees. Walk down to the river bank to see the Rangeet, but stay well back from the water's edge, as the current is strong. Then continue up to Tashiding. Seeing both on one day shows how Hindu and Buddhist traditions share the same valleys in West Sikkim.

faqs.q: Where is Kirateshwar Mahadev Temple
faqs.a: Kirateshwar Mahadev Temple is at Legship in Gyalshing district, West Sikkim, on the bank of the Rangeet river. Legship is a road junction on the way from Pelling or Gyalshing to Tashiding and Yuksom, and on the main road from Siliguri and Jorethang. It is an easy stop for anyone driving through.

faqs.q: What is the story of Kirateshwar Mahadev Temple
faqs.a: Hindu tradition says Arjuna did penance here and Shiva appeared to him in the form of a hunter, Kirateshwar, blessing him with success in the Mahabharata war. A stone revered as a Shiva linga is the main object of worship, and the complex also has shrines to Rama and Durga.

faqs.q: When are festivals held at Kirateshwar temple
faqs.a: The two main festivals at Kirateshwar Mahadev Temple are Bala Chaturdashi, in November or December, and Maha Shivaratri, in February or March. Both bring large crowds of devotees from Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills. Dates follow the Hindu lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Tashiding from Pelling
faqs.a: Tashiding is about 40 km from Pelling, 1.5–2 hours by road via Legship. By shared jeep, go from Pelling to Gyalshing (₹50–80), then Gyalshing to Tashiding (₹100–150), indicative, 2026. A reserved car is easier for families and lets you add Yuksom, which is about 19 km further on.

faqs.q: How far is Tashiding from Yuksom
faqs.a: Tashiding is about 19 km from Yuksom, around an hour's drive. Many travellers visit Tashiding on the way between Yuksom and Pelling, or as a half-day trip from Yuksom. Shared jeeps on this stretch are few, so a reserved car is the practical choice for most groups; agree the fare first.

faqs.q: Why is Tashiding Monastery important
faqs.a: Tashiding is one of Sikkim's most sacred monasteries. It was founded in 1641 by Ngadak Sempa Chenpo, one of the three lamas who crowned the first Chogyal at Yuksom in 1642, and it hosts the Bumchu festival, when a sacred vase is opened and its water read as an omen for Sikkim's year.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Tashiding
faqs.a: October to May is best, with dry roads and clear views. February or March is special if you can match your trip to the Bumchu festival, held on the 14th and 15th days of the first Tibetan month. From June to September, rain and landslides make the roads slow and views limited.

faqs.q: Is there a place to stay in Tashiding
faqs.a: Yes, but options are few and basic: a handful of simple lodges and homestays around the bazaar. They are useful during Bumchu or for an early start. Most travellers stay in Yuksom, an hour away, or Pelling, 1.5–2 hours away, where there is more choice across budgets.

faqs.q: Is Tashiding worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, for anyone interested in Sikkim's history and Buddhism. The hilltop monastery, its chortens and carved mani stones, and the views over two river valleys make a calm, rewarding half day. It also links the story of Yuksom's coronation to a working monastery founded by one of the three lamas.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Tashiding
faqs.a: Indian nationals do not need a permit for Tashiding, but should carry photo ID. Foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, which covers West Sikkim's main tourist places and is free, valid for 30 days and available online or at the Melli and Rangpo checkposts. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can you visit Tashiding, Yuksom and Pelling in one day
faqs.a: It is possible but long. Pelling to Yuksom is about 35 km, Yuksom to Tashiding about 19 km, and Tashiding back to Pelling about 40 km via Legship. Allow 9–10 hours with stops. We suggest staying a night in Yuksom and visiting Tashiding the next morning instead.

faqs.q: Are photos allowed at Tashiding Monastery
faqs.a: Photography is usually fine outside, among the chortens and mani stones, but ask before taking pictures inside the temple, where it may not be allowed. Avoid flash, and ask before photographing monks or pilgrims. During Bumchu, be extra careful not to block people or the ceremony with cameras.
